terms.definition: The number of building permits a state would issue over 2026-2030 if nothing changes: the average of the last three years (2023-2025) carried forward five years.
terms.section: The three layers and their units

terms.definition: The low and high ends around the baseline. In 80% of past five-year periods (every state, 1990-2015) the actual permit total fell inside a range this wide. It describes history, not a probability.
terms.section: The three layers and their units

terms.definition: What the source policy produced where it was measured (a California city's ADUs, Portland's middle housing, Los Angeles near transit), moved to this state's homes and lots, in the source's own unit. It does not subtract what current law already allows.
terms.section: The three layers and their units

terms.definition: The part of the benchmark that would be new in this state: the benchmark times the share of homes or lots the reform newly affects, phased in over the years, converted to building permits. This is the number to compare across reforms.
terms.section: The three layers and their units

terms.definition: Baseline plus increment, low with low, middle with middle, high with high.
terms.section: The three layers and their units

terms.definition: The unit a number is in. Numbers with different labels are never added together or ranked against each other.
terms.section: The three layers and their units

terms.definition: Building permits for new homes, as counted by the Census Building Permits Survey. The headline unit of this tool. A permit is not yet a finished home.
terms.section: The three layers and their units

terms.definition: Permits for new homes minus the homes demolished to make room for them (the unit of the missing-middle evidence).
terms.section: The three layers and their units

terms.definition: Homes finished and ready to live in (the unit of the ADU evidence from California).
terms.section: The three layers and their units

terms.definition: The change in the number of homes in an area, after any losses (the unit of the transit-oriented density studies).
terms.section: The three layers and their units

terms.definition: Permits estimated from a cost saving and how strongly builders respond to costs, rather than from a place that passed the reform. The parking and fee scenarios use it.
terms.section: The three layers and their units

terms.definition: A permit figure multiplied by how many homes get finished per permit. Shown beside ADU permits, because more permits per finished ADU raises permits, not homes.
terms.section: The three layers and their units

terms.definition: Three named choices for the assumptions that carry a scenario's evidence range. The low-to-high spread is a sensitivity range, not a probability.
The table of every assumption the model uses, each with its low, middle and high values, its source, the page or table it comes from, and the arithmetic.
The headline case: the newly affected share comes from the state's current law, with the scenario's phase-in and no delay.
A what-if you choose: 25%, 50% or 100% of homes or lots newly affected, starting after 0, 1 or 2 years.
The fraction of the homes or lots in the benchmark whose rules the reform would change, given what the state's law already allows.
How much of the benchmark reform a state's law already provides, from 0 (nothing statewide) to 1 (the same). The newly affected share is 1 minus current strength.

The file for each state and reform that records the statute, a quote, the effective date and a feature-by-feature comparison with the benchmark reform. States without a file are treated as having no statewide law.
Whether a person has checked a current-law record against the statute. "Pending" means not yet.

The share of a state's detached single-family homes inside the cities, towns and counties a law binds. Arizona's ADU law binds cities of more than 75,000 people and the areas outside cities, which hold 80% of its homes.

The one part of a reform without which nothing of it is in law: an ADU on every single-family lot, new rights for single-family lots, more density near transit, lower parking minimums, a fee cut. If a state's law lacks it, the current strength is 0 whatever else the law says.
Years with no activity before the reform starts producing homes; "starts after the horizon" means nothing within the five years.
The share of the full rate reached in each of the five years after a reform takes effect.
A chart that moves one assumption at a time from its low to its high value and shows how far the middle result moves. The longest bar is the assumption that matters most.
Every assumption at its most (or least) favorable end at once. An extreme for illustration, not a likely outcome.
When an assumption multiplies the result, the page recomputes it from the engine's own numbers with the same arithmetic as the engine. A test checks it against the engine to one part in a billion.
A value between two results the engine computed in advance (at the low, middle and high values), drawn on a straight line between them. Close, not exact; the command line gives the exact value.

If all five reforms passed together: the five increments added after removing the overlaps (lots near rail count once; parking and fee savings are one cost cut). An illustration; no study has measured the five together.
Rerunning today's baseline rule on past years and comparing it with what was actually permitted.
The share of past five-year periods whose actual total fell inside the range, counted separately for calm years, the 2005-2010 bust and the 2011-2015 recovery.
Redrawing the range each past year using only the years already known then, and checking it against what happened next.
A second way to draw the baseline range, from a teammate's earlier prototype: the last five years of permits stretched by the state's own slowest and fastest five-year stretches of the past 20 years.
The list of every check of the model, hits and misses, each with its evidence class, the prediction, what actually happened and where the outcome came from.

How much a check can prove. A frozen holdout tests the model; a calibration check is where a number came from, so it cannot also test it; an external check whose outcome was known beforehand is a scale check, not a blind test.

A check whose prediction (place, years, outcome, the model's range) was written down and fingerprinted (hashed) and the fingerprint committed before anyone fetched the outcome, so the prediction cannot be adjusted after the fact.

State-specific code that counts single-family parcels per county from a state or county parcel source, so the count can replace the national Census estimate. Counts only: no parcel rows, owner names or addresses.

A county's parcel count replaces the Census count only when the two are within 30% of each other; otherwise the Census count stays and the county is listed with its ratio, so one county's coding cannot drive a state result.
The Census Bureau's yearly count of homes by county. Shown as a consistency check beside the forecast, because the estimates are built partly from the same permits.
How many more homes get built over five years for each 1% fall in the cost of building, relative to the price of a new home. The one parameter behind the parking and fee scenarios.
A per-county version of the builder response built from how easily each metro area's housing supply grows. Shown beside the headline as a check: supply-constrained metros respond less.
Scales a source city's rate up or down by how this county's home values compare with the source city's, within fixed bounds.
One of five groups of California cities by median home value; each county elsewhere takes the ADU rate of the tier its own median value falls in.
A county that holds the core of a metropolitan area (the federal government's 2023 definition). The missing-middle estimate counts single-family homes in these counties.
A rail, streetcar or ferry stop. Bus and bus rapid transit do not count, because the national stop map cannot tell them apart.
Grade says what kind of evidence an assumption rests on (A measured, B derived, C judgment, R set by the challenge rules or a design choice); confidence says how far it transfers to another state.
The page, table or paragraph in a source where a number comes from.
Which release of a dataset was used (for example the 2020-2024 American Community Survey).
A code joining the commit of the code with a fingerprint of the inputs and the register, so any number can be traced to exactly what produced it.
Every sentence on this site that describes a result is a fixed sentence with the engine's numbers filled in. No language model writes any text.
A second, smaller home on a lot that already has a house: a backyard cottage, a garage apartment or a basement unit.
Buildings between a single house and a large apartment block: duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes and townhouses on lots now zoned for one house.
Allowing more homes near major transit stops.
A rule requiring a set number of parking spaces for each new home. Removing it lowers the cost of building where builders would otherwise provide fewer spaces.
Charges a locality levies on new homes. The challenge assumes $50,000 a home in total, cut in half.
